title: Efficient Matrix Product State Learning in Logarithmic Depth
claim: Prior methods apply a sequential chain of operations; ours organizes them in a parallel tree with logarithmic depth.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, top-to-bottom time flow, sequential staircase vs binary tree
description: Two quantum-circuit diagrams, labeled A and B in boxed letters. Panel A (left, narrow) shows the previous approach: vertical qudit wires with six unitary rectangles U_1 to U_6 stacked in a diagonal staircase. Each box is shifted right and lower than the last, so the circuit is sequential and deep. Green '0' labels mark ancilla outputs peeling off beneath each box, and the final state |ψ̂⟩ comes out at the bottom right. Panel B (right, wide) shows the proposed circuit as a binary tree. Eight first-layer unitaries U^1_i sit side by side, each under a bracket labeled B^1_i. Their surviving wires, labeled with tildes, feed 4 unitaries in layer 2, then 2 in layer 3, then a single U^1_4 at the bottom. Green zeros mark disentangled wires. Black line art with green accents. The eye goes to the wide, shallow tree in B, which contrasts with the long staircase in A.
caption: Comparison of circuit structures for MPS tomography. (A) Previous algorithms [ref] use a sequential circuit structure. (B) Our Algorithm [ref] produces a tree-like circuit structure, shown here for \(n=29\) and \(p=2\). Each rectangle represents a unitary \(U_i^j\), with \(j\) denoting the layer and \(i\) the unitary index within that layer. The vertical lines are qudits ordered from left to right, and time flows downward. The brackets mark the first-layer supports \(\mathcal{B}_i^1\), and the labeled wires mark the surviving sets \(\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}_i^j\) carried to the next layer.
abstract: Learning the closest matrix product state (MPS) representation of a quantum state enables useful tools for quantum machine learning and analysis of complex quantum systems. In this work, we study the problem of learning MPS in the following setting: given many copies of an input MPS, the task is to recover a classical description of the state. The best known polynomial-time algorithm, introduced by [LCLP10, CPF+10], requires linear circuit depth and $\widetilde O(n^5)$ samples, and has seen no improvement in over a decade. These costs, neither known to be optimal, renders existing algorithms impractical for near-term quantum devices with limited resources. We introduce parallel disentangling algorithms for MPS learning. For exact MPS learning, our algorithm runs in polynomial time and uses circuit depth $O(\log n)$ and sample complexity $\widetilde O(n^3)$, improving both the depth and the dependence on the system size $n$. The key idea is to exploit the bounded-rank structure of reduced states on middle blocks of an MPS and organize the disentangling operations in a tree structure. We further extend the algorithm to closest MPS learning, improving the sample complexity dependence on $n$ from $n^9$ to $n^7$ and complement the algorithms with an $Î©(n)$ product-state lower bound. We also investigate MPS learning under hardware constraints, including restricted measurements and geometric connectivity. Under the Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) assumption, we show computational hardness for learning an MPS(2) family with non-adaptive single-qubit measurements. Finally, we show that our algorithm can be implemented with depth $O(q n^{1/q})$ on a $q$-dimensional hypercubic lattice, giving an asymptotic reduction in depth. Together, our work provides a complete characterization of the quantum resources needed for efficient MPS learning.
